identification: John Campbell Pottery, Launceston. Shield-shaped wall pocket, catalogue height 18 cm (other examples measured 18 to 18.5 x 14.5 x 5.5 cm). Front: mottled emerald to aqua green glaze; relief koala in treacle brown clinging to a gum branch, two brown gumnuts above, leaves picked out in ochre yellow. Back: flat, olive yellow-green glaze with darker green runs at the edges, three stilt marks. No shape number, no date. The koala, nuts, branch and leaves are identical on the ten other examples I compared (Leski 2024 and 2026, Mossgreen 2009 x2 and 2016, Shapiro 2007 and 2015, Gowans 2011, eBay 2025 and 2026, Albion 2026), so the decoration is moulded, not hand-modelled; only the glaze colours change. Made after John Campbell's death in 1929, when his son Colin ran the pottery: about 1930s to 1950s. No dated example found. Condition from photos: pale angular marks on the front near the top rim, left of the gumnuts (possible glaze flake or chip, could be reflections); a dark brown spot on the side edge (right side from the front, left from the back): chip, kiln mark or glaze burn. No crack visible. Current bid $200 on 28 Nov 2026.
marks_seen: Incised script on the back: "John Campbell / Tasmania" (underlined) and lower down "K.B.L" (underlined). The cloud scan read K.B.C. The last letter is angular, and Shapiro read the same mark as 'K. B. L' on a green koala pocket in 2015 and 'Kbl' on another in 2007, so K.B.L is the better reading. It recurs on at least three green koala pockets, so it is a workman's mark or model code, not a one-off decorator signature, and adds nothing to value. Leski describe similar three-letter marks on other Campbell pieces as a workman's monogram. Gold oval label on the lower front with about four lines of print, not legible. String and Armitage lot tag through the hanging hole.

best_venue_to_sell: Leski Auctions, Melbourne (Australian & Historical sales): $600 for the same colourway on 21 Nov 2026 and $1,700 for the pink one in 2024. eBay Australia is the fallback at about $350 to $370 plus postage. A Brisbane general sale made $210. Tasmania is no better than the mainland for this piece: Armitage's own $480 sits inside the mainland range. Buyers are Australian pottery and koala/Australiana collectors bidding online, so a specialist auction beats a dealer. No dealer sold-pages found. Leski vendor commission not checked.
doubts: The $1,700 result is the pink colourway and does not carry over. Green is the common colour: 8 of the 11 examples with a known colour. Dated, linked green results are $600, $367, $350 and $210; $450 sits between the Leski result and the eBay pair. At $600 resale the max would be $254; at the eBay level it is under $100. Bidding was already $200 on 28 Nov, above the max. Condition is not confirmed. On a lot this small the 0.85 factor is probably generous once commission and freight are counted. The 2016 and 2015 results are over 10 years old. Trend: flat for green ($300 hammer in 2015, $210 to $600 in 2025-26); the pink has run away. The Kevin Power book (John Campbell Pottery: Recollections and Collections, 2014) covers the marks but is not online, so the K.B.L reading and the colour rarity rest on sale records, not on the literature.

The brown spot on the side edge: a chip through the glaze, or a kiln mark?

authenticity_note: Looks right on what can be seen, but that is three small photos and no provenance. The three-line corner inscription (title / Donald Friend / Bali) is his standard Bali form: Deutscher and Hackett 2017 lot 49 'Three Shy Nudes. / Donald Friend / Bali' (I compared the image: same layout, name followed by a comma, Bali set beneath), Lawsons 2025 'Nude Studies/Donald Friend/Bali', Leonard Joel 2025 'Nude studies', Bonhams 2016 'Boys from Kuta / Donald Friend / Bali'. A numeral in the title is recorded too: Christie's '3 Figures/Donald Friend/Bali'. Subject, medium and sheet size match his 1970s Bali figure sheets. I found no published list of Friend fakes or 'school of' works of this kind; that is absence of evidence, not clearance. Provenance lead: Wikipedia cites an Art Galleries Schubert (Queensland) page for a Friend titled 'Three Nudes' (file 3nude.htm, archived 28 Sep 2011 at web.archive.org/web/20110928032619/http://www.art-galleries-schubert.com.au/www/friend/3nude.htm). I could not open it; check whether it is this sheet. Labels seen on comparable works: Holdsworth Gallery, Art Galleries Schubert, Australian Galleries, Christopher Day Gallery, Von Bertouch Galleries (with exhibition dates), Barry Stern, Darlinghurst Galleries, Artarmon Galleries, Macquarie Galleries. They normally give artist, title, medium and a stock or catalogue number.
best_venue_to_sell: Lawsons (Sydney), Leonard Joel (Melbourne) or Davidson (Sydney). These three sold this type in 2023 to 2026 at $2,750 to $4,000 hammer. Deutscher and Hackett sold them in 2017 at $5,000 to $8,000 hammer, but I found no D+H sale of a Bali nude study since. Davidson vendor terms: 22% of the first $500 then 16.5% (GST included), 1.5% insurance, and the 5% artist resale royalty deducted where payable. It would be payable: Friend died in 1989 and you would have bought after June 2010. Davidson pay within 31 days of the sale. Lawsons and Leonard Joel vendor rates not published; ask. Allow 2 to 4 months from consigning to being paid, plus freight from Tasmania for a glazed frame.
doubts: The subject is the main risk. Friend's own diaries record that he sexually abused boys in Bali, and this sheet shows nude Balinese youths. The capital-city galleries hold his work but were reported in 2018 to have none on display; The Australian reported in 2017 that his works were often passed in or bought anonymously. Nude youth subjects still sell, but at roughly half the 2013 to 2017 level: the closest comp was estimated $7,000-9,000 in 2013 and made $3,200 hammer in 2025. Passes are common: Red Nude (Bali) twice in 2026, and a Reclining Nude, Bali unsold at $2,500 in 2022 then $600 in 2024. His clothed Ceylon portraits made $20,000 to $29,000 in 2025-26, so the weakness is in the nudes, not the artist. The money rule's 0.85 understates selling costs here: commission, insurance and resale royalty are about 24% before freight. On those costs the hammer that still leaves $200 is about $1,870, not $2,250. Size is unconfirmed: if 73 x 48 is the frame, the sheet is about 55 x 33 and resale is nearer $1,500. Davidson 'sold for' figures are taken as hammer; the page does not say. Shapiro 2020 $2,400 and Shapiro 2024 $11,659 from our earlier notes were not re-verified.
viewing_check: Measure the sheet (sight size). 73 x 48 should be the image, not the frame.

Back of the frame: gallery label (Holdsworth, Schubert, Australian Galleries, Christopher Day, Von Bertouch) or old auction lot number. A label lifts it and settles authenticity; a bare back means the selling house will vet it harder.
Under the glass: foxing or mould (the grey spots lower centre), fading of the ochre wash, cockling, mat burn, and whether the sheet is laid down on board.

identification: Edith Holmes (1893-1973), Tasmanian painter. Still life: branches of pink and white blossom in a squat green glazed jug with a handle, on a grey-green table with two fallen sprigs, against a dark blue-violet ground with red flecks. Early academic, tonal manner, not her later bright modernist colour. Catalogued as oil. It sits in a wide cream window mat in a distressed cream painted frame and looks glazed, so the support is probably board, card or paper. Catalogue size 42 x 36 cm fits the image (frame about 70 x 60 cm by photo geometry). No title or date visible. No bid yet on 28 Nov 2026 (opens at $1,000).
marks_seen: Signed lower right in thin dark script along the table edge, reads "Edith Holmes" (faint at this resolution). Printed card in a clear plastic sleeve fixed to the lower mat: postcard format, small logo top left, a block of about ten lines of small print on the left, four short lines in red at top right, a coloured strip along the bottom edge, and one handwritten line at bottom left after a small round mark. I zoomed both photos as far as they go and none of it is legible at 450 x 600 px. Best guesses, in order: (a) an estate card from the Glenorchy Antique Bazaar and Art Gallery exhibition of 10-25 Oct 1975, which Colville records as signed by Joan Dabrowski, the artist's executor; (b) a Hobart dealer's artist card with a stock code (Masterpiece Fine Art Gallery showed her in 1986 and 2002, Freeman Gallery used FG numbers); (c) a card from a tribute show (TMAG 'Edith Holmes, Dorothy Stoner: Two Retrospectives' 1983; Moonah Arts Centre 2003). Art Society of Tasmania and Tasmanian Group of Painters labels are normally on the back, not the mat. No photo of the back.

authenticity_note: Probably right. Signature position and form (lower right, 'Edith Holmes' in script) match catalogued works signed lower right (Colville 'Cherry Blossom's in Vase' 2023, GFL 'Still Life' 2023), and the subject and handling match the blossom still life Colville sold in Aug 2023. I could not compare letterforms at this resolution. No misattributions turned up in the sale record. There is a catalogue raisonne that Colville cites by number (Don and Maggie Row, 'A Catalogue Raisonne: Edith Holmes 1893-1973', Matroid Publications, 2009). Finding this picture in it is the proper check, and a catalogue number helps the resale.
best_venue_to_sell: Colville Auctions, Hobart. 33 of the 48 Holmes lots offered since May 2017 went through Colville, and her three highest hammer prices are theirs. Buyer's premium there is 20% plus GST; vendor commission is by agreement and not published, so ask (allow 15% to 20% plus GST, and the 5% resale royalty, since she died in 1973). Vendors are paid within 35 days. Sales run about four a year. Leonard Joel in Melbourne is the alternative and is patchier for still lifes: Pansies $5,500 in 2023, Gladioli $2,000 in Sept 2026.
doubts: Blossom still lifes are not her most sought-after work; they are close to her weakest line. Of 14 flower still lifes offered since 2017, 9 sold and 5 passed. They made $3,750 to $4,500 in 2017 to 2021 and $2,000 to $2,900 since 2023, with one outlier at $5,500. The trend is down. The best match (a larger blossom still life) passed at $5,000-6,000 in 2017 and sold for $2,700 in 2023. Someone appears to have tried this exact flip with the GFL dahlia picture ($2,200 in 2023) and it passed at Colville in 2025. Named Tasmanian landscapes are what sell: $9,000 twice, $6,500, $6,000, $5,500. All six figures in our notes are confirmed as hammer prices, but the Feb 2021 $3,200 is a landscape. Medium is not confirmed (a mat and glass on an 'oil'). The card is unread. Selling costs will run past the 15% in the money rule once the resale royalty is added. Armitage estimate is $2,000-3,000, which is retail for this subject, not trade.
viewing_check: Read and photograph the card on the mat and the whole back: labels (Art Society of Tasmania, Tasmanian Group of Painters, Glenorchy 1975 estate card signed Joan Dabrowski, Masterpiece or Freeman Gallery stock numbers), any title or date.
Confirm medium and support. Oil on board or canvas-board is what the comps are; oil on paper, or pastel, would sell lower.
Condition under the glass (flaking, mould, stained mat) and the signature under a loupe: painted in with the picture, not sitting on top.
